description:
We are building CubeSat Builder—an interactive web app that makes satellite design accessible to students! Users can drag-and-drop modular parts, order hardware from Amazon/Flipkart, simulate rocket launches, and track live GPS/weather data.
We are seeking student teammates interested in coding, web dev, UI design, hardware, weather science, and presentation pitching!

details:
What it does and how it works
Eyes on Earth is a cinematic, story-driven space mission design game for 1 to 4 players. Players run a small satellite agency responding to real past Earth events, such as a wildfire. Each mission follows a full lifecycle:

  1. Read the mission briefing and objective.
  2. Design a CubeSat from realistic parts (power, battery, computer, radio, camera, sensors) within limits on budget, mass, power, volume and data.
  3. Choose a launch vehicle and orbit, and see the trade-offs: image sharpness, revisit time, eclipses, ground-station passes and orbital lifetime.
  4. Fly live operations on a 3D globe, making real-time calls through eclipses, data downlinks and solar storms.
  5. Get a debrief with “failure forensics” that shows exactly which decision caused each problem, then redesign and fly again.

On success, players see the real satellite image of that event.

Benefits and intended impact
Mission trade-offs are usually abstract for students. The game makes them tangible: players feel the consequence of every engineering choice and learn by failing safely and trying again. Team mode gives each player an engineering role with competing goals, teaching negotiation and systems thinking. The game connects to a real Raspberry Pi-based CubeSat kit, turning players toward real engineering. Our goal is to inspire beginners and students worldwide to see themselves as future space engineers.

Tools and technology
TypeScript, Vite and Three.js (WebGL) for the 3D globe and visuals; Canvas 2D for gauges and charts; Web Audio for procedurally generated sound; GitHub Pages for hosting. Fonts: Syne, IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Serif, JetBrains Mono. Data: [NASA data you used]. Hardware: a Raspberry Pi-based CubeSat kit [status: planned / in development / tested]. AI tools: Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) helped write the code, Claude helped develop the concept, and Gamma was used for the slides.

Creativity
Instead of a parts builder with a score, the game is a story where every crisis in flight traces back to a design choice the team made earlier. Real events with fictional characters, all visuals drawn in code, and a bridge from game to real hardware make it unlike a typical educational game.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: realistic part data and simplified but real orbital physics.
  • Honesty: real images, fictional characters, and clear labels on the real satellite’s status.
  • Accessibility: colorblind-safe alerts, readable text and adjustable speed.
  • Age-appropriate design for beginners.
  • Performance: runs on ordinary laptops in a browser with no installation.
